item.title: Rust-Based CikaBika Bot Turns Discord into a Command Center
item.description:
CikaBika Bot uses fake documents to infect Windows systems, then abuses Discord and Ngrok to execute commands, spy on victims, and steal files.

Darktrace researchers have documented a new campaign distributing a remote access trojan called CikaBika Bot, written in Rust and controlled entirely through Discord. The infection chain starts with a disk image that looks like a business proposal, and ends with an attacker who can run arbitrary commands, steal files, and capture your screen, all through messages in a chat platform.

“The infection chain begins with a disk image and a malicious Windows shortcut. A Nim loader extracts the final payload and attempts to plant it in Microsoft Edge’s installation directory using a PowerShell UAC bypass.” reads the analysis published by Darktrace. “Once running, the RAT collects host information, registers the device with Discord, and accepts commands through a dedicated channel.”

The attackers use a disk image named Proposition_Projet.img as a lure; it contains two files, a PDF that appears to be a legitimate French-language document about writing summaries, and a Windows shortcut disguised as a Word document.

Open the shortcut and a hidden PowerShell process starts running in the background while the PDF displays on screen to keep the victim occupied.

The shortcut starts PowerShell, which reads the fake PDF as raw data. It uses a value hidden inside the file as a key to decrypt and extract a program, then saves it to a temporary folder. This program is a loader written in Nim, a programming language that is less common in malware than C. Attackers may use Nim because security tools are less familiar with it. The loader contains two more components: a Rust DLL and a PowerShell script.

The PowerShell script then tries to copy the DLL into Microsoft Edge’s installation folder and name it dbghelp.dll. This is the name of a legitimate debugging library that Edge normally loads. To access the protected folder without triggering a User Account Control (UAC) prompt, the script changes a Windows registry setting and misuses computerdefaults.exe to bypass the security check. Darktrace describes the technique as DLL search-order hijacking.

“The attacker appears to be exploiting this dependency through DLL search-order hijacking. However, it does not export every function in Edge’s delay-import table, meaning its compatibility with the host is incomplete.” the analysis continues.”The observed code establishes the intended sideloading route, rather than proving that Edge successfully loaded the planted DLL.”

However, the researchers note that the malicious DLL does not provide all the functions Edge expects, so this technique may not work on every system.

Assuming the implant lands and runs, it immediately registers the infected machine with Discord, creating a dedicated channel for that specific device. It then collects system information, runs tasklist and ipconfig, takes a screenshot, and sends everything back to the operator through that channel. The attacker gets a full picture of the machine within the first few seconds of infection.

The command set from there covers most of what an attacker would need. Remote shell access, process listing and termination, file upload and download, and surveillance functions including screenshot capture, camera access, and screen streaming.

“Once installed, CikaBika Bot uses Discord as its C2 platform, allowing the attacker to manage compromised devices, execute commands, and retrieve files without maintaining dedicated C2 infrastructure.” the cybersecurity firm states. “The observed use of Discord channels for individual victims, alongside additional data exfiltration through ngrok, shows how legitimate services can be repurposed to support malicious operations.”

Discord is a legitimate service used by millions of people and organizations every day. Traffic to Discord doesn’t look unusual on most networks, it’s not blocked by default, and standard endpoint security tools aren’t designed to treat Discord messages as potential command-and-control traffic. The attacker never has to spin up a dedicated server, register a suspicious domain, or deal with infrastructure that can get taken down. They just need a Discord account.


One drawback for attackers is that Discord can detect abuse and shut down the accounts and servers they use. However, creating new accounts is easy and costs very little. The attackers also use Ngrok to transfer files instead of sending large amounts of data through Discord. This reduces their reliance on Discord and limits the impact if the platform shuts down their accounts.

“CikaBika Bot demonstrates how attackers continue to rely on social engineering techniques to deliver malware.” concludes the report. “Although the initial distribution method has not been confirmed, the use of a disk image containing a shortcut disguised as a Word document, alongside a legitimate-looking PDF, suggests the campaign was designed for phishing.”

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, malware)

item.title: SECURITY AFFAIRS AI-CYBERSECURITY NEWSLETTER ROUND 4
item.description:
Security Affairs AI-CYBERSECURITY newsletter includes a collection of the best articles and research on AI in the international landscape

Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing cybersecurity, reshaping both the techniques used by attackers and the tools available to defenders. AI agents can automate tasks, analyze large amounts of data, discover vulnerabilities and accelerate offensive operations. At the same time, AI is creating new capabilities for threat detection, incident analysis and response. Security Affairs’ new newsletter follows this evolution, covering every week the latest threats, attacks, vulnerabilities and developments at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity.

item.title: 16-Year-Old Broadcom Wi-Fi Bug Lets Attackers Take Over Routers Without a Password
item.description:
A Broadcom Wi-Fi flaw dating back to 2010 allows attackers within Wi-Fi range to execute code on vulnerable routers without authentication.

Researcher Quentin Kaiser presented a talk at Hexacon in Paris documenting a vulnerability in Broadcom’s proprietary 802.11 implementation that has been present in their SDK since at least 2010. The bug allows an attacker to get unauthenticated remote code execution on affected routers without knowing the WiFi password or going through the normal WPS setup process.

As of October 15, 2026, none of the affected devices in Belgium had received a patch.

“A vulnerability affecting Broadcom’s proprietary implementation of 802.11 has been present in their SDK since at least 2010. An incomplete patch was silently released in 2018, followed by Broadcom’s recommendation to move to hostapd instead, making it a definitive forever day on eCos-based platforms (BCM3380, BCM3383, BCM33834) and a potential forever day on Linux platforms (BCM3390, BCM65xx, BCM68xx) unless affected Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) are willing to migrate.” states Kaiser. “The vulnerability can be triggered remotely over WiFi without knowledge of the network key or completion of a normal WPS enrollment. Exploitation provides controlled information disclosure and arbitrary code execution.”

The vulnerability affects the WPS EAP reassembly code, which handles part of the wireless setup process used by many consumer routers. An attacker within Wi-Fi range can exploit the flaw without knowing the Wi-Fi password, completing the setup process, or requiring any action from the user. The attack can expose information and allow the attacker to run code on the router. In his demonstration, Kaiser extracted the Wi-Fi password from the router’s memory and sent it over the wireless connection. He then used the password to connect to the network.

These attacks are not just theoretical. Kaiser demonstrated working exploits against two devices: the Orange Belgium ASKEY TCG3000 and the Proximus Sagemcom F@st/BBOX3V+. Both allowed an attacker to run code without authentication. In one demonstration, the attacker opened a reverse shell using only Wi-Fi frames, without needing a command server accessible over the internet. The attack can work from a distance. The close antenna placement shown in the video was only for the laboratory setup and is not a requirement for the attack.

In the video below, Kaiser exploited an Orange Belgium router (ASKEY TCG3000). The attack allowed him to run code on the device without authentication. The code retrieves the Wi-Fi password (PSK) from the router’s NVRAM and sends it back to the attacker over Wi-Fi. He then used the stolen password to connect to the network, confirming that the exploit works and that the password is correct.

Do not be misled by how close the antenna is in the video. The attack can work over much longer distances.

In the next video, the researcher exploited a Proximus router (BBOX3V+, also known as Sagemcom F@st). This attack also allows code execution without authentication. He used it to open a reverse shell over Wi-Fi frames, without needing a command-and-control (C2) server hosted in the cloud.

Broadcom quietly released an incomplete fix in 2018, then told customers to migrate to a different software stack entirely rather than shipping a complete patch for their own code. On eCos-based platforms, covering chipsets like BCM3380, BCM3383, and BCM33834, that makes this a permanent unfixable bug by design. On Linux-based platforms (BCM3390, BCM65xx, BCM68xx) the situation depends entirely on whether individual manufacturers decide to act.

Kaiser reported the bugs to Broadcom in July 2026. Broadcom said a patch was available and told him to ask the affected device manufacturers to contact Broadcom directly. The company refused to assign a CVE or share the notification it had sent through its customer portal. CERT/CC opened a case but closed it the same day after confirming that Broadcom could assign CVEs itself and had no intention of doing so. This was not a proper disclosure process. It was a dead end, with a paper trail.

Kaiser’s rough calculation, done with Belgian telecom market data, puts the affected device count at around 850,000 for Proximus, 500,000 for VOO’s legacy fleet, and 210,000 for Orange Belgium, totalling somewhere north of 1.5 million potentially exposed gateways in one small country. Telenet may also be affected through Sagemcom devices but Kaiser couldn’t confirm because he couldn’t get hold of one.

The affected manufacturers sell into markets well beyond Belgium. The chipsets in question appear in devices across dozens of vendors and hundreds of products worldwide. Kaiser is publishing a fingerprinting script and a YARA rule specifically to help map the full scope of affected deployments, because right now nobody has a complete picture.

A vulnerability introduced in 2010 and only partly fixed in 2018 still affects routers in use today. Kaiser says AI-assisted analysis helped him find the bugs in less than a week, instead of months. This can help defenders find vulnerabilities faster, but attackers can do the same.

The risk is greatest in targeted attacks where an attacker is within Wi-Fi range, such as hotel network attacks or surveillance of nearby targets. Compromised routers are difficult to monitor, and attackers can quietly intercept or collect network traffic. Most users and security teams rarely check the firmware on ISP-provided routers.

“Although I could have done this research by myself, it would have taken me months to get there. With AI frontier models it took me less than a week.” Kaiser concludes. “Which is a good thing because we can start looking into deeper and deeper layers of our technical infrastructure for a fraction of the cost.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Broadcom Wi-Fi)

item.title: Japan’s SiteGuard WAF flaw CVE-2026-106931 is already being exploited (2026)
item.description:
Attackers are exploiting vulnerability CVE-2026-106931 in SiteGuard Server Edition to run commands as root or SYSTEM.

EG Secure Solutions published an urgent alert warning of CVE-2026-106931, an OS command injection bug in SiteGuard Server Edition. Threat actors are already exploiting it in the wild. A successful exploit lets them run commands with root or SYSTEM privileges on the server where the product runs.

SiteGuard is a Japanese web application firewall (WAF) that runs directly on the web server it protects. The vulnerability affects its statistics feature, which is enabled by default.

The vendor and JVN rated the vulnerability with a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.5 and a CVSS 3.0 score of 7.8. An attacker needs local access and low-level privileges to exploit this vulnerability. This suggests the flaw may be used after an attacker has already gained access to a system.

The vulnerability impacts version 2.20 or later. On Apache, Nginx and IIS that means anything before 8.00 Update 5, except FreeBSD, and on FreeBSD with Apache or Nginx it means anything before 7.00 Update 6. IIS editions from 3.10 through 4.00 Update 4 aren’t affected, and only installs with the statistics function enabled are exposed.

For people who can’t upgrade their version, the vendor offers a patch that replaces the files used in statistics processing, and it covers end-of-life versions too.

Be aware that updating or patching can erase the traces of an attack, so the vendor tells administrators to download the diagnostic information first.

“Before updating, please be sure to download and save your “Diagnostic Information” (as this may erase traces of the attack).” reads the vendor’s advisory.

In the web management screen that’s the diagnostic information page, then the download option. Do it before you touch anything, because a clean server after the update doesn’t prove it was clean before.

The timeline is short, but not everyone was warned at the same time. The vendor says it notified customers with direct support contracts on September 29. The public alert and the JVN advisory were published on October 14. The vendor reported the vulnerability to Japan’s IPA, while JPCERT/CC coordinated the disclosure and published its own alert. Customers without direct support contracts received the warning about two weeks later.

Many details remain unknown. Neither advisory identifies the attackers or victims, explains how the attacks were carried out, or says how many systems were affected. The vendor has confirmed that the vulnerability has been exploited. If you use this product, check your systems for signs of compromise and investigate any suspicious activity.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, SiteGuard WAF)

item.title: Attackers Abuse Stolen ConnectWise Application Credentials to Target Microsoft 365
item.description:
Attackers stole ConnectWise application credentials to access Microsoft 365 tenants, prompting the company to suspend cloud services.

ConnectWise suspended its Cloud Backup service and took both SaaS Security and Cloud Management offline over the weekend after discovering that unknown attackers had obtained unauthorized access to seven of its application identities.

The company discovered the incident on October 14 through internal monitoring, disabled the compromised identities on October 17, and is still investigating how attackers obtained the credentials.

“We have taken protective action following unauthorized access to application identities associated with ConnectWise Cloud Backup, formerly known as SkyKick. Our investigation remains ongoing. Since implementing the mitigations described below, we have not observed successful threat activity in the environments we monitor.” reads the alert published by the company on October 17. “Out of an abundance of caution, we suspended Cloud Backup service by revoking certificates used for affected application connections across all users. This removed ConnectWise’s access through those connections. The shared credentials previously used for Cloud Backup are no longer valid and cannot be used. In addition to mobilizing our internal security teams and Security Operations Center (SOC), we have engaged a reputable third-party incident response firm to support our investigation and containment efforts. Together, these teams are actively monitoring our backup infrastructure and broader environment, with the investigation extending across all partner-facing services. At this time, we have no indication that any other ConnectWise product, service, or offering is impacted.”

This was not a case of attackers stealing individual customers’ passwords. ConnectWise’s applications already had permission to access customer Microsoft 365 environments to manage services and run backups. After stealing the application credentials, the attackers could pretend to be ConnectWise’s own applications and request access tokens from Microsoft Entra ID. They did not need to steal any customer passwords.

Depending on the permissions granted to these applications, the attackers could access mailboxes, SharePoint documents, Teams messages, and directory data. ConnectWise explained that disabling the affected connections prevents new authentication through those connections; however, it does not reverse changes previously made inside a tenant. In other words, disabling the compromised connections stops new access through them, but it does not undo what the attackers may have already done inside customer environments. Any changes made before the connections were disabled may remain.

Here’s what makes this particularly hard to clean up. An attacker who used a stolen application credential to get into a tenant could add their own client secret to a different trusted application already registered in that tenant, or create an entirely new application and grant it permissions. Either path gives them a second key that still works even after ConnectWise’s original compromised credential is revoked.

“The larger risk is what happens when that access is used to gain more. If an application can assign directory roles, as we saw in one tenant, it can make itself a Global Administrator, and an administrator can add credentials to other applications, create new applications and grant them permissions, reset passwords and authentication methods for users, and change Conditional Access policies.” reads the analysis published by cybersecurity firm Huntress. “Each of those steps gives the attacker another way back in that does not depend on the original vendor credential, which is why rotating the vendor credential is necessary, but not enough.”

Huntress identified malicious sign-ins from IP address 144.172.64.128 through October 15 at around 14:20 UTC, and a second targeted wave later that same day aimed specifically at 16 tenants in the policy, national security, trade, and critical minerals sectors. That second wave appeared to be manual rather than automated and hit Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Teams, Azure Resource Manager, Entra, and Office 365 Management APIs in rapid succession. All 16 attempts in the second wave failed, but the fact that they were manually targeted at sensitive sectors is the detail worth sitting with.

Of about 1,000 Microsoft Entra tenants that recorded sign-in activity from the suspicious IP address, around 300 sign-ins were successful. However, a successful sign-in did not always give the attackers access to a tenant. In some cases, they could not proceed because the required service principal was missing. This was a result of the tenant’s configuration, not a security measure that had been deliberately put in place.

ConnectWise said its Cloud Backup archives remain encrypted, isolated, and preserved, with no evidence that attackers accessed or compromised them.

“Cloud Backup remains suspended. Scheduled backups are not running, and access to affected backup archives and restoration capabilities remains unavailable.” continues the ConnectWise’s alert.”Existing archives remain encrypted, isolated, and preserved. We have no evidence that these archives have been accessed.”

However, while the service remains offline, backups cannot run and customers cannot restore their data. This creates an operational risk for organizations that depend on the service to recover their systems and information.

Huntress’s recommendation for anyone using ConnectWise Cloud Backup or Cloud Management is to review both their own Microsoft 365 tenant and every managed customer tenant, including any with dormant SkyKick connections. Look specifically for sign-in activity from 144.172.64[.]128 starting October 13. Before doing anything else, preserve available sign-in and audit logs, because containment steps can overwrite the evidence you need to understand what actually happened.

The list of what to check is long: application credentials and federation trusts, directory role assignments, consent grants, recent policy changes, mailbox forwarding rules, and delegated mailbox access. Any of these could be the thing an attacker quietly added before the connection was killed. Full ConnectWise advisory and ongoing updates are available here.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, ConnectWise)

item.title: Big Fish: OpenBSD Root Exploit Chains a 37-Year-Old BSD Bug With a Kernel Flaw
item.description:
OpenBSD flaws, including a 37-year-old BSD bug, enable local attackers to bypass security protections and gain root access. Patches are available.

Cybersecurity firm Calif published a full exploit and write-up this week for a local privilege escalation on OpenBSD 7.9 that chains two separate kernel flaws, one of them a 37-year-old integer overflow inherited from the original BSD sources. The exploit bypasses OpenBSD’s KARL address randomization and the SMAP and SMEP hardware protections without needing any information disclosure vulnerability at all.

OpenBSD already shipped patches for both issues in September: the integer overflow fix in errata 018 on September 14, and the related use-after-free fix in errata 026 on September 30. Both are available through syspatch and cover all architectures.

The shared memory attachment counter, shm_nattch, was defined as a signed 16-bit integer in BSD source code in 1988. It could hold a maximum value of 32,767. OpenBSD inherited this definition and never changed it. By mapping 127 shared memory segments and creating 259 processes through forking, an attacker can push the counter beyond its limit, causing it to wrap around to a negative value. This triggers a use-after-free vulnerability through a race condition. The corrupted counter makes the kernel free memory that other processes are still using.

The second flaw builds on the first. An out-of-bounds write overwrites multicast membership counters in the kernel. When the affected socket closes, the resulting counter updates modify page table entries, allowing user memory to be accessed with supervisor-level privileges. This bypasses SMAP and SMEP protections by exploiting errors in the kernel’s internal memory accounting, rather than directly attacking the hardware.

“One traced back roughly 37 years to the original BSD sources, where a shared memory attachment counter was defined as a signed 16-bit short. Repeatedly forking a process with shared memory attachment records could push that counter past its maximum value of 32,767, causing it to wrap to a negative value.” reads the Califs’ analysis. “This integer overflow could lead to a use-after-free via a race condition; combined with a separate out-of-bounds write in the kernel, it allowed local privilege escalation to root.”

OpenBSD’s KARL protection relinks the kernel at boot to randomize function and data addresses, which is real and meaningful hardening.

“While OpenBSD’s KARL relinks the kernel binary to randomize both function and data addresses, the kernel’s memory allocators remain deterministic. Both the boot-time allocator and the best-fit allocator lack base address randomization.” continues the analysis. “Consequently, early boot allocations consistently land at predictable locations across boots on the same hardware.”

Early boot allocations, including function pointers in network interface handlers, land at the same addresses across every reboot on the same hardware.

That predictability is what the exploit actually uses. It targets the lo0 and enc0 interface ioctl handlers, two structures the kernel always places at known addresses, overwriting one to gain code execution and using the other to cleanly restore the overwritten pointer afterward. No information disclosure needed, no guessing required.

The researchers used kernel memory allocation metrics available through sysctl to track live allocations and detect when new pages were being created, essentially doing heap layout analysis from userland. They aligned IP socket allocations and set a multicast TTL option to a non-default value to get a persistent 16-byte structure placed where they needed it. The race condition was won by using IPC_RMID in one process while a helper process running in parallel attached a size-confused shared memory segment.

Calif researchers note there’s no evidence of either flaw being exploited in the wild, and no CVE has been assigned to either issue as of publication.

The report does more than explain the exploit. Calif suggests four security improvements that could make this attack much harder or prevent it entirely.

First, safe-unlinking for kernel linked lists checks that data structures are valid before writing to memory. If something is wrong, the kernel stops. FreeBSD and NetBSD already use this protection, but OpenBSD does not.

Second, randomizing the page table’s self-referential mapping at boot would prevent attackers from predicting which memory location to target with the decrement operation.

Third, randomizing the kernel allocator’s base address at boot would make it harder to predict function pointer locations. The researchers say this protection would have almost no performance cost.

Finally, enabling array bounds checks in release builds would detect this type of out-of-bounds write. Calif also reported 21 issues to FreeBSD that the same protection could have caught, including flaws that could allow local privilege escalation.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, OpenBSD)

item.title: Deepfakes and Election Manipulation: UK Watchdog Seeks Faster Detection
item.description:
The UK Electoral Commission is building an AI system to alert candidates to damaging deepfakes within three hours.

The UK’s Electoral Commission is building an AI-powered system to tell candidates about significant deepfakes within three hours of posting. Its chief executive, Vijay Rangarajan, said so at a panel at the Conservative Party’s annual conference last week, as Tech Policy Press points out that it’s a rare public intervention from a man who has run the regulator since 2024 and who mostly speaks to Parliament in evidence sessions.

He began with an example from another country. During Ireland’s 2025 presidential election, a deepfake video falsely showed candidate Catherine Connolly saying the election had been cancelled and that she was withdrawing from the race. The video also urged her supporters not to vote. None of this was true, and Connolly went on to win the election.

Rangarajan said a similar video during a UK election could influence a significant number of votes. However, he stressed that the Electoral Commission has clear limits to its role. It does not settle disputes over political claims made during a campaign. Its focus is on false statements that could disrupt the election process itself.

““If that happens to the British election, that will move a significant amount of votes,” he said, adding that it was not the Electoral Commission’s role to arbitrate rival claims made by candidates during the cut and thrust of a campaign, but rather to focus on statements such as this one that could undermine the administration of the election itself.

“To address that risk, the commission conducted a pilot program during the UK’s local elections in May 2026, Rangarajan said. “We ran a full pilot, analyzed about three million posts through an AI,” he explained. “So, this is a good example of how AI can work: 147 bits of content were flagged. Humans then looked at those — not a terribly pleasant job in some cases — ten were really quite misleading, and we referred to the social media companies or to the police.”” Tech Policy Press reports.

The Commission has tested the idea. During the local elections in May 2026 it ran a full pilot, and an AI analyzed about three million posts. It flagged 147 pieces of content, humans reviewed them (he called that unpleasant in some cases), and ten were really quite misleading, so they went to the social media companies or the police.

Rangarajan said the posts had little impact. However, the trial showed that the Electoral Commission now has a system to help voters, journalists and political parties deal with deepfakes. He expects attempts to use them to disrupt UK elections. The pilot began earlier in 2026 and monitored fake audio and videos designed to mislead voters about the election process or falsely show candidates doing or saying things. The Commission said it would publish the results.

The system has a clear focus. Identifying and prosecuting the people behind deepfakes can take weeks or months, often long after an election. Instead, the Commission aims to act without first identifying who created the content. AI scans social media posts in real time and flags suspicious material for human review. If a post meets the required criteria, the Commission alerts the relevant candidates or parties, ideally within three hours of its first appearance. Rangarajan said this is roughly the time it takes for content to go viral.

That narrow scope has edges. Full Fact, whose AI tools were monitoring more than a thousand candidates in the May elections, found a Glasgow candidate’s campaign videos built with AI. The Commission told Full Fact the clips fell outside its pilot because each was labeled an illustrative AI scene, even though the label sat at the end of the caption.

The legal backdrop is the real problem. Rangarajan said the Commission was set up for money and people, and now it’s all about information, so it has to work out how laws from 1983 or 2000 apply in 2026. Earlier this year the Guardian reported, according to a summary on the Resilient Media for Democracy Observatory, that the Commission was seeking legally enforceable takedown powers from the government.

Then there’s the part with no legal answer at all. Rangarajan said he believes at least one social network showed signs of algorithmic bias at election time, though he didn’t name it. His scenario is a platform that changes its recommendations during an election without warning, suggesting neighbors with one political view and suppressing others, so users think their neighbors have changed their minds.

The Commission believes it has already detected some algorithmic bias in social media campaigns, but Rangarajan said UK law offers no clear solution. Experts and campaigners have also raised concerns about X’s role in UK politics and TikTok’s Chinese ownership.

The Commission faces 30,000 to 40,000 cyberattacks a month, sometimes reaching 10,000 a day, including botnet attacks and phishing. Rangarajan wants stronger, more independent security capabilities and believes major social media monitoring could be handled by another body.

Tech Policy Press sees his comments as a call to update election laws and possibly create new offenses. The next general election must take place by August 2029, but it could be called earlier, and it remains unclear whether lawmakers will act in time.

For now, what the Commission has is a three-hour promise and a pilot that worked at small scale.

Rangarajan describes the threat it’s meant for as “an absolutely certain attempt to use some of these deepfakes against the UK.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Deepfakes)

item.title: Meta wants to scrape your website to train its AI, and you can’t say no
item.description:
Meta wants the right to scrape your website for AI training. If you have a business account, that includes you.

At the end of the month, Meta plans to change its commercial terms in a way that matters to every company advertising or selling through its platforms. The new language takes effect on October 30, 2026. It lets Meta collect content from websites associated with business customers and use it to train AI models or otherwise improve its products, according to The Register.

Meta defines “business customer” broadly. It includes anyone who uses ads or marketing messages, sells or lists products, develops apps, uses a product catalog, manages a Page, runs a Group for business purposes, or uses tools such as Ads Manager or Meta Business Suite. At least one million businesses already use Meta’s AI agents in WhatsApp and Messenger. Nieman Lab also points out that almost every news publisher has at least one Meta business account.

The contract clearly explains which tools Meta can use. By accepting the terms, you allow Meta, or anyone working on its behalf, to use automated tools such as web scrapers, bots, spiders and crawlers to access and index your websites, pages and URLs. These tools can also revisit your sites regularly to collect updates.

“You authorise us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyse, collect, retrieve or crawl the domains, web pages or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages or URLs.” states Meta’s commercial terms. “Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.”

Then comes the use clause. The company may use any content from those domains to provide, develop, improve, research, train and maintain the integrity of its products, services and features. The contract lists scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers and user agents, which is a lot of ways to say visitor you didn’t invite.

The News/Media Alliance says there’s no way out. Business accounts have no option to opt out of the terms, and the only alternative is to stop using Meta’s products.

““Meta’s new commercial terms of use are outrageous and probably illegal. The company’s decision to withhold access to its audience unless businesses allow Meta to scrape content from their websites is an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power. It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30.” states Media Alliance. “The text is so far reaching that any business with intellectual property online and a Meta business account could have their copyrighted material taken from them.”

Danielle Coffey, President and CEO of the News/Media Alliance also pushed the point beyond news sites. Her questions were whether Taylor Swift’s Meta business account would give Meta access to copyrighted media on her website, and whether Shutterstock’s would let Meta scrape its images. The Alliance’s argument is that any business with intellectual property online and a Meta account could be affected, not just publishers.

There is also a problem with robots.txt. News reports say the social network giant plans to let businesses control how its crawlers access their websites through robots.txt files, but the contract makes no such promise. The law does not always require companies to follow these instructions, so businesses must rely on Meta to respect their preferences.

The company didn’t respond to The Register’s request for comment.

If you run a Meta business account, someone should read the terms before October 30 and check what your own robots.txt actually says.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, AI)
item.content:encoded:
Meta wants the right to scrape your website for AI training. If you have a business account, that includes you.

At the end of the month, Meta plans to change its commercial terms in a way that matters to every company advertising or selling through its platforms. The new language takes effect on October 30, 2026. It lets Meta collect content from websites associated with business customers and use it to train AI models or otherwise improve its products, according to The Register.

Meta defines “business customer” broadly. It includes anyone who uses ads or marketing messages, sells or lists products, develops apps, uses a product catalog, manages a Page, runs a Group for business purposes, or uses tools such as Ads Manager or Meta Business Suite. At least one million businesses already use Meta’s AI agents in WhatsApp and Messenger. Nieman Lab also points out that almost every news publisher has at least one Meta business account.

The contract clearly explains which tools Meta can use. By accepting the terms, you allow Meta, or anyone working on its behalf, to use automated tools such as web scrapers, bots, spiders and crawlers to access and index your websites, pages and URLs. These tools can also revisit your sites regularly to collect updates.

“You authorise us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyse, collect, retrieve or crawl the domains, web pages or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages or URLs.” states Meta’s commercial terms. “Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.”

Then comes the use clause. The company may use any content from those domains to provide, develop, improve, research, train and maintain the integrity of its products, services and features. The contract lists scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers and user agents, which is a lot of ways to say visitor you didn’t invite.

The News/Media Alliance says there’s no way out. Business accounts have no option to opt out of the terms, and the only alternative is to stop using Meta’s products.

““Meta’s new commercial terms of use are outrageous and probably illegal. The company’s decision to withhold access to its audience unless businesses allow Meta to scrape content from their websites is an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power. It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30.” states Media Alliance. “The text is so far reaching that any business with intellectual property online and a Meta business account could have their copyrighted material taken from them.”

Danielle Coffey, President and CEO of the News/Media Alliance also pushed the point beyond news sites. Her questions were whether Taylor Swift’s Meta business account would give Meta access to copyrighted media on her website, and whether Shutterstock’s would let Meta scrape its images. The Alliance’s argument is that any business with intellectual property online and a Meta account could be affected, not just publishers.

There is also a problem with robots.txt. News reports say the social network giant plans to let businesses control how its crawlers access their websites through robots.txt files, but the contract makes no such promise. The law does not always require companies to follow these instructions, so businesses must rely on Meta to respect their preferences.

The company didn’t respond to The Register’s request for comment.

If you run a Meta business account, someone should read the terms before October 30 and check what your own robots.txt actually says.

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, AI)

item.title: Plex2Shell Exploit Used to Turn Vulnerable Plex Servers Into Crypto Miners
item.description:
Attackers exploit Plex2Shell flaws to install crypto miners and proxy software. Admins should update their Plex Media Server.

Plex Media Server is designed to make movies, music, and other media available across devices. But when a server is exposed to the internet and runs vulnerable software, it can become an entry point for attackers who have little interest in your film collection.

On October 16, 2026, security researcher Zach Main published technical details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code for a vulnerability chain dubbed Plex2Shell. Within a day, researchers had observed attackers using the exploit against an internet-facing honeypot, deploying cryptocurrency-mining malware and proxy software. The incident is a reminder of how quickly a public exploit can be weaponized by threat actors.

The chain combines four vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server: CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656. Together, they can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable servers without valid credentials, provided the required conditions are met. The code runs with the privileges of the Plex service, giving attackers an opportunity to install additional software and abuse the host.

The technical details are available in Main’s original analysis, Plex2Shell. Plex had been notified of the vulnerabilities on July 27 and acknowledged the report on August 4, awarding a bug bounty. The company released fixes in September, before the exploit code became public.

The loader does not check the library’s name, executable permissions, digital signature, or symbols. As a result, the library’s ELF constructor can run with the same privileges as the Plex service.

“It doesn’t check for a lib prefix, doesn’t require the execute bit, doesn’t verify any signature, and doesn’t look for any specific symbol.” reads the report published by zmain.com. “When dlopen loads a shared object, it runs the ELF’s DT_INIT_ARRAY (constructor functions) before doing any symbol resolution. A .so that only has a constructor and no exported symbols will still execute its code on load. We then trigger a second transcode. The codec directory gets re-enumerated, the .so we wrote in Stage 4 gets loaded, and the constructor runs as uid=1000(plex).”

That detail matters because the final stage can exploit how Plex loads shared libraries. The chain uses a setting related to transcoding to influence execution, allowing a specially crafted library to run when Plex loads it. The result can be code execution under the service account, without requiring the attacker to obtain an interactive login first.

The first confirmed activity appeared on October 17, when a researcher monitoring a vulnerable Plex honeypot reported seeing exploitation in the wild.

“My honeypot mostly saw scanning and generic exploitation attempts. As of this morning (Oct 17th), I finally saw in the wild exploitation.” reports the researcher on BoredHackerBlog. “So by default, I don’t allow outbound traffic from my honeypots but due to how this vuln works, I had to go modify my settings later on so sadly I didn’t get payloads for all the attacks. It’s possible that I have partial data. I haven’t gone through pcaps and I had to modify settings for tcpdump anyway. The attacker could be using slightly modified code & technique too.”

The attackers used the publicly available exploit to deploy an XMRig-based cryptocurrency miner. Later that day, the researcher found a second payload named myawesomeproxy, which turns the compromised system into a proxy node and may allow others to use its internet connection.

Cryptomining consumes computing resources and electricity, while proxy software creates a different risk. Attackers can route traffic through compromised residential or business connections, potentially using their reputation and IP addresses to reach services or networks that might otherwise block suspicious infrastructure. A Plex server can therefore become more than a source of unwanted costs: it can provide an attacker with a foothold for further activity.

Plex released patched versions in September, and administrators should ensure they’re running Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 or later. This includes installations running on NAS devices, virtual machines, and Docker containers. Updating the application is the immediate priority, particularly for servers exposed directly to the internet.

Administrators should also investigate unexpected child processes launched by Plex, unexplained CPU usage, unfamiliar files in the Plex Codecs directory, and outbound connections to unrecognized IP addresses. The appearance of cryptocurrency miners or proxy processes deserves particular attention. Because attackers can change filenames, infrastructure, and payloads, detection shouldn’t depend on a fixed list of indicators alone.

The honeypot findings provide evidence of exploitation, but they don’t establish how many real-world systems have been compromised or identify the operators with certainty. Organizations should treat the activity as a warning to check exposure and patch promptly, rather than assume that every vulnerable server has already been attacked.

“I wouldn’t be surprised if threat actors deploy more sophisticated things. Plex may be hosted on residential IP and I think threat actors would love to have residential IP proxy to access corporate VPNs and emails. (edit: see update at the bottom. i do see proxy being deployed now)” the researchers adds.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Plex2Shell )
